hey <@U0A6088AMM3>,
Thanks for the detailed report. To confirm the root cause could you help with the following?
*Memory at the time of the crash* 
Right after the pod is killed, run this on the node where it was running and share the output:
```dmesg -T | grep -iE "out of memory|oom-kill|killed process" -A3```
This can help identify which process was killed (`java` or go) and its memory usage at the time of the OOM event.
*During the sync, capture process memory every 5 seconds:*
```while true; do
  date +%T
  kubectl exec <sync-pod> -- ps -eo pid,rss,comm --sort=-rss | head -5
  sleep 5
done```
Alternatively, a Grafana graph of `container_memory_working_set_bytes` for the sync pod would help.
*Additional information needed:*
Output of `kubectl describe pod <sync-pod>`.
Output of `kubectl describe node <node>`.
Were any other pods running on the same node during the sync?

text:
Hi <@U08CR7HUWDC> ,
I have shared a detailed analysis of job that failed yesterday. Can you have a look?

Context: OLake v0.12.0 (olakego/source-postgres:v0.12.0), OLake UI + workers on GKE. Source migration / public.lenskart_last_year_cases (Postgres 18.4) → Iceberg lenskart_migration_db.lenskart_last_year_cases via REST catalog (Lakekeeper 0.10.4) on Wasabi S3 (ap-southeast-1). Full refresh, max_threads: 2, retry_count: 5, Standalone (no CDC), legacy writer (arrow_writes not set).

Why this table is unusual — this is the crux:
rows            : 78,523,153
heap            :    16 GB
TOAST           : 4,488 GB      <- ticket_response + conversation_response (jsonb)
indexes         :    23 GB
total           : 4,527 GB
avg JSON/row    : ~131 KB  (ticket_response ~39.5 KB + conversation_response ~79.7 KB)
total on wire   : ~10.3 TB

1. Kernel OOM dump — the node was recycled since, but GCP's serial-console log has the dmesg output verbatim:
olake invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0x100cca(GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE), order=0, oom_score_adj=993
CPU: 7 UID: 0 PID: 690600 Comm: olake Not tainted 6.12.94+ #1
memory: usage 29037432kB, limit 29029444kB, failcnt 403935
oom-kill:constraint=CONSTRAINT_MEMCG, oom_memcg=/kubepods.slice,
  task_memcg=/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/kubepods-burstable-pod501d708c_cc30_41e0_94e0_092157c5c263.slice/...,
  task=java,pid=690688,uid=0
Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 690688 (java)  total-vm:30703192kB, anon-rss:12007688kB, pgtables:24472kB, oom_score_adj:993
Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 690561 (olake) total-vm:13169024kB, anon-rss:11671996kB, pgtables:23264kB, oom_score_adj:993
Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 690600 (olake) total-vm:13169024kB, anon-rss:11671996kB, pgtables:23264kB, oom_score_adj:993
Both processes were killed, each holding ~11.5 GiB:
• java (Iceberg writer) — anon-rss 11.45 GiB, total-vm 29.3 GiB
• olake (Go connector) — anon-rss 11.13 GiB
• combined ≈ 22.6 GiB

Two details worth noting: the kill was at oom_memcg=/kubepods.slice (limit 27.7 GiB) — the node's pod-allocatable cgroup, not a container limit, because the sync pod has no memory limit, so nothing capped it earlier. And oom_score_adj: 993 falls out of the 256Mi request vs 22 GiB actual usage.

2. Memory over time — from cAdvisor (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace="olake", pod=~"sync.*", image!~".*kafka.*"}); scanning all of 2026-10-11 returns exactly one series, this pod:
time (UTC)   working set     RSS
01:00:10        0.00 GiB   0.00 GiB
01:00:20        0.81 GiB   0.60 GiB
01:00:40        2.38 GiB   2.17 GiB
01:00:50        5.68 GiB   5.46 GiB
01:01:00       13.97 GiB  13.74 GiB
01:01:20       17.99 GiB  17.74 GiB
01:01:40       22.13 GiB  21.87 GiB   <- last sample; killed at 01:01:33
0 → 22 GiB in ~90 seconds (~250 MB/s), starting the instant the two backfill threads began reading. cAdvisor's 22.13 GiB and the kernel's 22.58 GiB agree to within 2% from independent sources.

Correlating with olake.log:
01:00:08  Dropping Iceberg table: lenskart_migration_db.lenskart_last_year_cases
01:00:11  Started shared Iceberg JVM on port 50051
01:00:12  Starting backfill for stream[lenskart_last_year_cases] with 9 chunks
01:00:12  created writer for chunk min['(1048576,0)'] max['(1310720,0)']
01:00:12  created writer for chunk min['(0,0)']       max['(262144,0)']    # max_threads=2
01:01:31  Successfully wrote 8361 events for thread: ... across 0 files    # 27,086 ms gRPC call
01:01:33  <OOM kill>
01:01:36  worker.log: pod failed (exit code: 137, reason: OOMKilled)
state.json: {}                                                            # nothing checkpointed
So one batch of 8,361 records had landed with a second in flight — roughly 2 GB of source bytes in flight produced ~22.6 GiB of RSS (~11x amplification). across 0 files says the writer was still accumulating in heap.

Small note on your ps snippet: the connector image (eclipse-temurin:17-jre-noble) ships without procps, so ps -eo pid,rss,comm doesn't work inside the pod — we had to read /proc/<pid>/status. Might be worth adding for debuggability.

3. Pod / node
• Pod: requests: 256Mi / 100m, no limits, QoS Burstable, restartPolicy: Never, exit 137 at 96 s.
• Node: 8 vCPU / 32 GB, 28.9 GiB allocatable, kubepods.slice limit 27.7 GiB, kernel 6.12.94+, otherwise idle.

4. Other pods on the node during the sync — yes, but all small:
olake        sync-123-146-…  (this job)      17.99 GiB @01:01:30 (peak 22.13)
olake        sync-123-141-…  (Kafka sync)     3.45 GiB
lakekeeper   lakekeeper-69768bc894-zxdjj      1.08 GiB
kube-system  6 daemonsets                    ~0.21 GiB total
≈4.7 GiB was already in use; the sync pod took everything left.


Our reading of the code (v0.12.0 — please correct us):
1. drivers/postgres/internal/backfill.go sizes ctid chunks as constants.EffectiveParquetSize (2 GB) ÷ block size → 262,144 blocks, derived from relpages, i.e. heap only. With 16 GB heap but 4,488 GB of TOAST, "9 chunks" is really ~8.7M rows / ~500 GB of JSON each.
2. destination/writers.go:253 flushes at 10k records or MaxDestinationBatchBytes (1 GB). At 131 KB/row the byte cap wins: 8,361 × 131 KB ≈ 1.07 GB — matching the log exactly.
3. destination/iceberg/iceberg.go:146 picks legacywriter unless arrow_writes is set, so that whole batch crosses gRPC and is expanded in JVM heap.
4. destination/iceberg/java_client.go:188 launches the writer with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0; with no container limit that's computed against the node's 32 GB → ~24 GB ceiling, so G1 expands instead of collecting.
5. protocol/sync.go:122 runs ClearState + DropStreams for full-refresh streams on every run — hence state.json: {} and a restart from zero (plus a re-dropped destination) on each attempt.

text:
hey <@U0BTUQGHDDF>,
There's no issue with your selected streams. The DDL statements in the log (`DROP TEMPORARY TABLE ... temp_order_summary_*` and similar) are on other tables in the same MySQL instance, not on the tables you're syncing. OLake logs every DDL it sees in the binlog, which is why these lines show up, but they don't affect your sync or your data.

Hey <@U08CR7HUWDC>  thanks,  Two things:
1. Memory sizing: the table is ~4.5 TB (78.5M rows, ~131 KB of JSON per row). The failed run peaked at 22.6 GiB RSS (java 11.45 + olake 11.13) with max_threads: 2, after only one 8,361-record batch had flushed. What would you recommend allocating — and does that peak stay bounded, or keep growing as the run progresses? Our sync pods get requests: 256Mi with no limits, Can we set resources per-job?
2. Resume on failure: if a full refresh dies midway, can it continue from where it stopped? Ours restarts from zero each attempt (state.json: {}, destination re-dropped). For a one-time dump of this size (~50 h run), is incremental with an int cursor + append_mode the right pattern instead?

text:
<@U0A6088AMM3>
*1.* You can create a 64 GB pod for now. We're already working on a feature to configure sync pod resource limits, which will be merged soon. You can track its progress here: <https://github.com/datazip-inc/olake-helm/pull/218|github.com/datazip-inc/olake-helm/pull/218>
*2.* We support resumable full loads. However, to resume from the point of failure, you need to select either *Full Refresh + CDC* or *Full Refresh + Incremental* mode.
